question:
Patient note:
A 44-year-old man, right-hand dominant and previously working as an air-traffic-control technician, was sent to the cardio-oncology consultation service this afternoon by his primary medical oncologist because of progressive exertional breathlessness, early satiety, and intermittent confusion that have complicated ongoing systemic therapy for an advanced malignancy. He was diagnosed eighteen months ago with a sigmoid adenocarcinoma after presenting to an outside emergency department with iron-deficiency anemia and a positive fecal immunochemical test; staging at that time already revealed multiple bilobar hepatic deposits on contrast-enhanced CT as well as two sub-centimeter pulmonary nodules, and he ultimately underwent laparoscopic segmental colectomy followed by six cycles of oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, after which disease assessment showed stable liver lesions but interval enlargement of the lung nodules. Pembrolizumab was initiated nine weeks ago in an effort to control the metastatic spread, and his most recent PET–CT obtained last month demonstrated persistent FDG uptake in the liver coupled with several new foci within the L2 vertebral body. Throughout the past year he has noticed progressive lower-extremity edema, nocturnal cough relieved by extra pillows, and a 15-pound unintentional weight gain, findings that were attributed to anthracycline exposure during an earlier short-lived clinical-trial regimen. A transthoracic echocardiogram performed two weeks ago documented a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 32 % with global hypokinesis and mild mitral regurgitation; there is no history of sudden chest pressure, diaphoresis, emergent catheterization, or enzyme-positive infarction, and serial electrocardiograms remain free of Q waves or dynamic ST–T changes. He denies calf cramping when walking the grocery aisles, has never undergone vascular bypass or endovascular stenting, and ankle–brachial indices measured at a community health fair last summer were 1.04 bilaterally. Respiratory review is notable only for occasional dry cough thought to be medication-related; he has never smoked, never required inhalers, and baseline spirometry performed before chemotherapy revealed normal lung volumes with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.81. Over the past six months family members have become concerned that he repeats questions, forgets scheduled laboratory appointments, and misplaces personal electronics around the apartment; neuropsychologic testing arranged by occupational medicine last week disclosed deficits in recent memory and executive function out of proportion to his educational background, with preserved language comprehension and visuospatial skills, raising suspicion for treatment-accelerated neurocognitive decline on a background of presumed early-onset degenerative disease first hinted at by subtle word-finding pauses three years earlier. He follows a predominantly plant-based diet after receiving nutritional counseling during oncology visits; fasting plasma glucose at last week’s clinic draw was 99 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 5.7 %, and he has never taken metformin, sulfonylureas, or insulin. Previous electronic records contain no episodes of gastroduodenal hemorrhage, Helicobacter pylori therapy, or chronic proton-pump-inhibitor use, and he has not endorsed dyspeptic pain, melena, or occult blood on recent fecal testing beyond the tumor-related bleed that led to diagnosis. Liver function panels obtained this morning show aspartate aminotransferase 34 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 30 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 118 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 3.9 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.1, values essentially unchanged from baseline despite the extensive parenchymal replacement by tumor. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 92 mL/min/1.73 m², blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, indicating preserved renal handling. Vital signs in clinic: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg seated in the left arm, pulse 96 beats/min irregularly irregular at times, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air; body-mass index is 26 kg/m². He appears younger than stated age yet fatigued, with periorbital puffiness and mild temporal wasting. Jugular venous pulsation rises to 7 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, the point of maximal impulse is displaced laterally, and auscultation reveals a soft S3 with no murmurs or pericardial rub. Bibasilar lung fields are clear to mid-back but mild scattered crackles emerge on forced expiration. The abdomen is soft and nondistended with a well-healed infra-umbilical laparoscopic port scar; the liver edge is smooth, palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, and moderately firm, while the spleen tip is not felt. There is 2 + pitting edema to mid-shin without skin discoloration, and pedal pulses are full. Neurologic examination shows an alert man oriented to person and place but uncertain of the exact date; mini-cog testing yields recall of one out of three objects at five minutes, and clock-drawing depicts misplaced numbers despite correct circle size. Cranial nerves II–XII are intact, strength is 5/5 throughout, coordination is preserved, deep-tendon reflexes are 2 + and symmetric, plantar responses are flexor, and tandem gait is performed slowly but without deviation. Current medications include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily started after the low-ejection-fraction finding, furosemide 40 mg each morning, lisinopril 5 mg daily, pembrolizumab every three weeks, vitamin D3 1000 IU daily, and ondansetron as needed for chemotherapy-related nausea; he reports no drug allergies, does not consume alcohol, and never used illicit substances. The referring oncologist requests guidance on optimizing volume status, adjusting cardioprotective therapy in the face of ongoing immunotherapy, and assessing capacity to participate in consent discussions for future metastatic-disease clinical trials, while the patient expresses hope to continue part-time remote work and maintain autonomy in daily living despite worsening forgetfulness and cardiorespiratory limitations.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums weighted comorbidities, counting only the highest applicable severity within each disease category.
- Metastatic solid tumor: sigmoid adenocarcinoma with hepatic metastases = 6. The primary tumor is not scored separately.
- Congestive heart failure: orthopnea, edema, an S3, and LVEF 32% = 1.
- Dementia: the progressive memory and executive deficits with functional impact support counting the presumed degenerative neurocognitive disorder = 1.
- Other comorbidities = 0. Hepatic metastases do not by themselves establish chronic liver disease. Age 44 adds no points even if age adjustment is used.
Sum: 6 + 1 + 1 = 8.
Final answer: 8
